name: CTranslate2
baseline: PyTorch 1.13.1 (OpenNMT-py, Hugging Face Transformers), TensorFlow 2.11.0 (OpenNMT-tf), Marian 1.11.0, FasterTransformer 5.3 (GPU)
workload: Translating the En-De newstest2014 test set with Transformer base models (OpenNMT-tf WMT14, OpenNMT-py WMT14, OPUS-MT/Marian); target tokens generated per second, aggregated over several runs, CPU with 4 threads and GPU.
claimed_speedup: CPU, OpenNMT-py WMT14 model: CTranslate2 3.6.0 658.8 tokens/s vs OpenNMT-py/PyTorch 275.8 (about 2.4x, derived from page data); int8 860.2 vs PyTorch int8 323.3. CPU, OPUS-MT model: CTranslate2 525.0 vs Transformers/PyTorch 147.3 (about 3.6x, derived) and vs Marian 344.5 (about 1.5x, derived). GPU, OPUS-MT model: 5876.4 vs Marian 3241.0 and Transformers/PyTorch 1022.9 tokens/s. GPU, OpenNMT-py model: fp32 CTranslate2 6634.7 vs FasterTransformer 5.3 at 6979.0 (CTranslate2 slower), but CTranslate2 float16 10990.7 vs FasterTransformer float16 8592.5. Max memory also lower (CPU OPUS-MT 721MB vs Marian 7605MB).
hardware: CPU: 4 threads on an AWS c5.2xlarge instance, Intel Xeon Platinum 8275CL. GPU: AWS g5.xlarge, NVIDIA A10G, driver 510.47.03, CUDA 11.
stars_or_usage: 4.7k stars; on PyPI as ctranslate2 4.8.2 (2026-08-31); backend of faster-whisper
tradeoffs: Supports a fixed list of Transformer architectures only (encoder-decoder, decoder-only LLM, encoder-only); models must first be converted to its own format; int8/int16/float16 quantization changes outputs slightly (BLEU 26.64 to 26.82 in the table); CPU backends are third-party (Intel MKL, oneDNN, OpenBLAS, Ruy); C++ and Python APIs.
caveats: First-party README benchmark; the README itself says results are valid only for the configuration used. Benchmarked versions are old (CTranslate2 3.6.0 vs repo release 4.8.2; PyTorch 1.13.1, TensorFlow 2.11.0, early 2023), so the ratios may have changed. Compiler and flags not stated (prebuilt wheels). Benchmark scripts are public under tools/benchmark in the repo (not opened). Baselines are general-purpose frameworks, not tuned inference engines, except Marian and FasterTransformer, which CTranslate2 only partly beats. faster-whisper (SYSTRAN) is a Python wrapper over this engine and should fold into this entry.
found_via: PyPI JSON page https://pypi.org/pypi/ctranslate2/json (native C++ extension package) and WebSearch 'faster than XNNPACK C++ OR C github inference engine' (CTranslate2 in results); not in vcpkg or conan-center (config.yml 404).

name: Adept-2
baseline: CppAD (measured in the benchmark); autodiff (autodiff/autodiff, measured); ADOL-C and Sacado (named in the user guide, qualitative)
workload: Time to compute all sensitivities (reverse-mode adjoint AD) for four quant-finance workloads: Heston Monte Carlo (8 sensitivities), SABR calibration (15), XVA CVA (40), LIBOR swaption (161).
claimed_speedup: Gradient time, Adept vs CppAD: Heston MC 91 ms vs 268 ms; SABR calibration 19 ms vs 32 ms (autodiff 38 ms); XVA CVA 7.1 s vs 8.0 s; LIBOR swaption 1.15 s vs 4.57 s (about 2.9x, 1.7x, 1.1x, 4.0x, derived from page data). autodiff did not finish (DNF) on three of four workloads. XAD, the benchmark owner's own library, is faster than Adept in every row, so Adept is the second-fastest tape library there. The Adept user guide says reverse-mode differentiation 'tends to be significantly faster and use less memory' than ADOL-C, CppAD and Sacado, and usually only a little slower than a hand-written adjoint (no numbers in the guide; numbers are in Hogan 2014, ACM TOMS 40, 26).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3, -O3 -mavx2 -mfma on all libraries, median of 10 measured iterations after warmup (ad-benchmarks README)
license: Apache-2.0 (library); GNU all-permissive license for test and benchmark code
stars_or_usage: 189 stars; used in climate and weather codes (ECMWF)
tradeoffs: Operator-overloading AD with expression templates; Adept 2 adds array classes and optimizers; autotools build; reverse mode records a tape; optimized BLAS recommended for matrix work.
caveats: The A-tier benchmark is run and published by Xcelerit, the vendor of XAD (a competing library that wins every row), so it is a competitor's benchmark of Adept; ADOL-C and Sacado are not in it. The original claim is in the peer-reviewed Hogan 2014 ACM TOMS paper, which I could not open here (the user guide at doc/adept_documentation.tex only states it qualitatively); verifiers should open that paper for the 2014 numbers. The Adept margin over CppAD is small on XVA CVA (7.1 s vs 8.0 s). Last upstream commits are small additions (Oct 2025).
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ automatic differentiation library benchmark faster than CppAD ADOL-C Adept' surfaced the ad-benchmarks repo; vcpkg has cppad but no adept port, conan has neither (config.yml 404).

name: ik_llama.cpp
workload: llama-bench style prompt processing (PP) and token generation (TG) in tokens/s on an 8B LLaMA-3 model in BF16/F16 and several quantization types, CPU only.
claimed_speedup: AVX2 (Ryzen 7950X, 16 threads PP, 2 threads TG): PP BF16 256.90 vs 78.58 t/s (3.269x), Q8_0 268.19 vs 147.92 (1.813x), Q5_0 251.21 vs 111.68 (2.249x), Q4_0 273.54 vs 153.52 (1.782x), IQ3_S 156.47 vs 30.20 (5.181x); TG 1.05x to 2.10x (Q4_0 12.92 vs 11.23 t/s). ARM NEON (M2-Max, 8 threads PP, 4 threads TG): PP F16 91.24 vs 28.96 (3.151x), Q8_0 129.70 vs 54.54 (2.378x), IQ3_S 80.89 vs 11.49 (7.040x); TG 1.000x to 1.238x. Quote: on the Ryzen-7950X the slowest quantization type in ik_llama.cpp is faster than the fastest type in llama.cpp for prompt processing.
tradeoffs: Fork last synced with upstream in August 2024, so it lacks newer mainline features and models unless ported; adds its own quantization types (some GGUF files from other tools, e.g. Unsloth _XL, do not work); only the CPU (AVX2 or better, NEON or better) and CUDA (Turing or newer) backends are performant, ROCm/Vulkan/Metal are not supported; gains are mostly in prompt processing (compute bound), token generation is memory-bandwidth bound and close to mainline.
caveats: Author's own comparison in a GitHub discussion, no compiler or flags stated, discussion date not captured; mainline llama.cpp has kept improving, so the ratios are against the mainline of that time. README only says 'in many cases, better performance' and 'much faster CPU prompt processing for all non-interleaved quants'. Fork with substantial performance-relevant kernel changes (new GEMM/GEMV kernels, interleaved quants, FlashMLA).
found_via: WebSearch 'ik_llama.cpp fork faster CPU inference than llama.cpp benchmarks prompt processing tokens per second' (after vcpkg/conan llama-cpp and ggml ports showed no baseline numbers in the upstream READMEs).

name: ByteTransformer
workload: BERT-base (standard BERT encoder) inference execution time in ms on one A100, fp16, batch size 1 and 16, average sequence length 0.6 times the maximum, maximum sequence length 64 to 1024.
claimed_speedup: Batch 16, max sequence length 1024: ByteTransformer 24.70 ms vs PyTorch 53.21, TensorFlow 65.94, FasterTransformer 50.28 (45.22 with remove-padding), DeepSpeed 59.96 (about 2.2x vs PyTorch and 1.8x vs FasterTransformer with remove-padding, derived from page data). Batch 1, max 1024: 3.16 ms vs PyTorch 4.2, TensorFlow 6.37, FasterTransformer 4.51, DeepSpeed 4.86.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA 11.6, PyTorch 1.13.0+cu116, Python 3.9.16; cmake -DTORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=8.0 -DDataType=FP16; nvcc optimization flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA A100 (host CPU model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 481 stars; deployed in ByteDance in-house serving
tradeoffs: Only the standard BERT transformer encoder is supported; padding-free algorithm for variable-length inputs; C++ and Python/PyTorch plugin APIs; NVIDIA GPUs only (V100, T4, A100 compute capability).
caveats: Peer-reviewed at IEEE IPDPS 2023 (stated in the README; the paper itself was not opened here). The README tables show ByteTransformer is not always the fastest: at batch 1 and sequence 192 FasterTransformer is faster (1.26 vs 1.36 ms), and at batch 16 and sequences 64 and 256 to 384 FasterTransformer with remove-padding is faster (e.g. 6.47 vs 7.49 ms at 320). Benchmark script benchmark/bert_bench.sh is public (not opened). Compiler flags and host CPU not stated, so not A.
found_via: Direct README lookup while surveying transformer inference kernel libraries after the vcpkg/conan/PyPI listings; no registry hit (not in vcpkg or conan).

name: LightSeq
baseline: PyTorch fp16 mixed precision (training and inference), PyTorch QAT
workload: Training and inference speedup for Transformer and BERT models, relative to PyTorch fp16 mixed precision; training on one A100, inference on eight A100.
claimed_speedup: Headline: fp16 training up to 3x vs PyTorch fp16; int8 training up to 5x vs PyTorch QAT; fp16 and int8 inference up to 12x and 15x vs PyTorch fp16 inference. Tables: Transformer inference batch 32, sequence 8: 11.82x fp16 and 14.44x int8; BERT inference batch 1, sequence 32: 10.51x fp16 and 11.30x int8; BERT inference batch 32, sequence 128 only 1.82x fp16; Transformer training 1.44x to 1.99x fp16, BERT training 1.59x to 2.12x fp16.
hardware: NVIDIA A100 (one for training, eight for inference)
tradeoffs: Custom fused CUDA kernels on top of cuBLAS/Thrust/CUB; Transformer-family models only; Fairseq, Hugging Face and DeepSpeed compatibility; PyPI wheels only for Python 3.6 to 3.8 on Linux.
caveats: First-party README numbers, no compiler, flags or CPU stated; the headline 'up to 3x' training figure does not match the README tables (largest listed fp16 training speedup is 2.12x; the larger figures may be in docs/performance.md, not opened). Baseline is PyTorch 2022-era. Repository archived July 2025, so the project is read-only.
found_via: PyPI JSON page https://pypi.org/pypi/lightseq/json (package with CUDA extension); not in vcpkg or conan.

name: FasterTransformer
baseline: TensorFlow XLA (FP16), PyTorch TorchScript (FP16), FasterTransformer FP16 baseline
workload: BERT-base encoder inference on a T4 in FP16, varying batch size and sequence length, relative to TensorFlow XLA and PyTorch TorchScript.
claimed_speedup: README text: versus TensorFlow XLA FP16 on T4, about 3x speedup for small batch size and sequence length, and about 5x for large batch and sequence using Effective FasterTransformer with INT8-v2; versus PyTorch TorchScript FP16, 4x to 6x speedup for small sizes (CustomExt) and about 5x for large sizes with INT8-v2. Effective FT and INT8-v2 each give about 2x over FasterTransformer FP16 for large cases and 3.5x combined.
hardware: NVIDIA T4 (FP16); other GPUs in docs/bert_guide.md (not opened)
tradeoffs: Built on CUDA, cuBLAS, cuBLASLt and C++; TensorFlow, PyTorch and Triton backends plus C++ examples; FP16, INT8, FP8, tensor and pipeline parallelism; GPU only.
caveats: The numbers are in figure images referenced from the README, so only the README's text summary is quoted; no compiler or flags, framework versions not given in the quoted text. NVIDIA states development moved to TensorRT-LLM; the repo stays up without further development. Benchmark scripts (benchmarks/bert/*.sh) are public but were not opened.
found_via: Direct README lookup; named as a baseline in the ByteTransformer README; not in vcpkg or conan.

name: Marlin (FP16xINT4 LLM matmul kernel)
baseline: FP16 matmul (cuBLAS-class dense GEMM) and other popular 4-bit inference kernels
workload: FP16 x INT4 (group size 128) matrix multiplication for LLM inference at batch sizes 1 to 32, on a large matrix and on layer shapes of popular open-source models at batch size 16.
claimed_speedup: README text: close to ideal 4x speedup over FP16 weights, with the maximum possible 3.87x speedup (0.125 bit group-scale overhead) held up to batch sizes around 16 to 32 tokens, whereas existing 4-bit kernels degrade quickly as the batch size grows beyond 1 to 2 tokens. The per-kernel numbers are in plot images (assets/peak.png, models.png, sustained.png) that were not read.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA 11.8 or newer nvcc matching the torch version; no optimization flags stated
hardware: NVIDIA A10 GPU for the peak comparison; other Ampere/Ada GPUs for model layers; sustained test at locked base GPU clock
tradeoffs: Ampere/Ada only (compute capability 8.0 or higher), not optimized for Hopper; weight-only INT4 quantization; PyTorch extension (marlin.Layer, marlin.mul).
caveats: First-party README; the comparison against named other kernels is only in images, and the speedup is stated relative to the theoretical ideal rather than against a named baseline kernel. The README links to an arXiv paper (not opened here). Written in CUDA with a PyTorch extension, so not directly a C++ library API.
found_via: Direct README lookup while surveying GEMM/quantized kernel libraries after the registry listings; not in vcpkg, conan or PyPI search results.

name: tiny-cuda-nn
baseline: TensorFlow v2.5.0 with XLA (which uses cuDNN/cuBLAS)
workload: Training and inference throughput (elements per second) of fully fused multi-layer perceptrons 64 and 128 neurons wide, batch sizes 2^14 to 2^21.
claimed_speedup: README plot 'Fully fused networks vs. TensorFlow v2.5.0 w/ XLA' (values read off the image, approximate, derived from the plot): for the 64-wide MLP at batch 2^21, inference about 1.08e9 vs about 1.4e8 elements/s (about 8x) and training about 2.0e8 vs about 1.0e8 (about 2x); the gap is larger at small batches (training about 1.2e8 vs about 1.2e7 at 2^14). README text: automatic JIT fusion gives a further 1.5x to 2.5x over the library's own non-JIT path.
stars_or_usage: 4.5k stars; used by Instant NGP and NerfStudio
tradeoffs: Fully fused MLPs work for narrow layers only (up to about 128 neurons; JIT fusion can slow larger models and older GPUs); NVIDIA GPU, CUDA 10.2+ (Linux), C++17, CMake 3.21+; PyTorch bindings add overhead (about 2x slower at batch 64k than native CUDA).
caveats: Numbers exist only as a plot image, so ratios are my reading of the figure. The benchmark code is public (benchmarks/bench_ours.cu, bench_tensorflow.py, data/config_oneblob.json, not opened) and hardware is named, but compiler and flags are not, so it falls short of A. The baseline TensorFlow 2.5.0 is from 2021. The linked technical paper (Mueller et al., SIGGRAPH 2021) was not opened. The README speedup against its own non-JIT path is not an external-baseline claim.
found_via: Direct README lookup (PyPI tinycudann returned 404, so no registry hit); not in vcpkg or conan.

name: OneFlow
baseline: PyTorch 1.6, TensorFlow 1.x/2.3, MXNet 1.6, PaddlePaddle 1.8.3, MindSpore, and NVIDIA NGC PyTorch/TensorFlow/MXNet containers
workload: DLPerf training throughput on 4 nodes with 8 Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB each: ResNet-50 v1.5 (images/s) and BERT-base pretraining (sentences/s), FP32 and automatic mixed precision.
claimed_speedup: ResNet-50 v1.5 FP32 bsz=128: OneFlow 12411.97 img/s vs NGC PyTorch 10917.09, NGC MXNet 11233.92, PyTorch 10021.29, NGC TensorFlow 1.x 9514.64, TensorFlow 2.x 9418.44 (about 1.14x vs NGC PyTorch, derived from page data). AMP bsz=256: OneFlow 33141.02 vs NGC MXNet 30713.68, NGC PyTorch 22551.16, NGC TensorFlow 1.x with XLA 29171.69 (about 1.47x vs NGC PyTorch, derived). BERT-base AMP bsz=max: OneFlow 15724.70 vs NGC TensorFlow with XLA 11650.0 and NGC PyTorch 10349.12 (about 1.52x, derived).
hardware: 4 nodes x 8 Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB (host CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Full deep learning framework (PyTorch-like API, global tensors, graph compiler); the speed claim is an end-to-end training result that mixes kernels, scheduling and communication, not a kernel library result.
caveats: The benchmark is run by the OneFlow vendor (DLPerf repo of Oneflow-Inc), versions are from 2020-21 (OneFlow v0.2.0, PyTorch 1.6, TensorFlow 2.3), baselines use each framework's stock example scripts, and OneFlow's margin over NGC MXNet in FP32 is small (about 1.1x); PyTorch AMP is missing from the table. Compiler and flags not stated. Scripts and reports are public in DLPerf (not opened beyond the README).
found_via: PyPI JSON page https://pypi.org/pypi/oneflow/json, then the OneFlow-Inc/DLPerf README; not in vcpkg or conan.

name: faster-enhancer.c
baseline: ONNX Runtime (fp32 ONNX graph of the same FastEnhancer-Medium weights)
workload: Streaming speech enhancement at 48 kHz with FastEnhancer-Medium (320-sample frames), hand-written int8 SIMD GEMM kernels for NEON, DOTPROD, I8MM and x86 AVX2/VNNI versus the ONNX Runtime graph.
claimed_speedup: GitHub repository description: '3.3x faster than the ONNX Runtime graph, same quality'. README: real-time factor 0.069 on one Apple M2 core and 0.096 on a Galaxy S23+, 565,108-byte weights blob, quality PESQ 3.054 (int8) vs 3.060 (fp32 ONNX) on 824 VoiceBank-DEMAND utterances. The ONNX Runtime timings behind the 3.3x figure are not in the README text.
compiler_and_flags: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; compiler and flags not stated
hardware: Apple M2 (one P-core) and Samsung Galaxy S23+ (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2); x86 tiers not timed
tradeoffs: Runtime for one fixed model, not a general library; no scalar fallback (fails at init without the baseline ISA); allocation-free after init; byte-identical output across kernel tiers within an architecture family.
caveats: Very small, new repo (4 commits at last look). The 3.3x claim is only in the repo description; hardware and flags behind it were not stated, docs/optimizations.md says artifacts for the ONNX benchmarks sit under experiments/ but that directory was not found in the repository. Paper is a preprint (arXiv:2607.25350), not opened. The author notes that paced real-time use costs 4.2x more per frame than the racing benchmark. Kernel patterns were informed by ggml/llama.cpp, XNNPACK, oneDNN and KleidiAI.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ library faster than XNNPACK OR oneDNN inference kernels benchmark GitHub' (result faster-enhancer.c).

name: RTNeural
workload: Single-sample real-time-factor (48 kHz audio) of Dense, Conv1D, GRU, LSTM layers and activations at layer sizes 4 to 64, RTNeural compile-time and run-time APIs with Eigen, xsimd and STL backends vs libtorch, ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite.
claimed_speedup: Results are PNG plots in RTNeural-compare (values read off the images, approximate, derived from the plots). LSTM layer size 4: RTNeural Eigen (static) about 270x real time vs ONNX Runtime about 1.4x and libtorch about 0.38x; at size 64: about 6.5x vs about 1.1x and about 0.27x. Dense layer size 4: RTNeural xsimd (static) about 6000x vs TensorFlow Lite about 150x, ONNX Runtime about 7.5x, libtorch about 2.3x; at size 64: about 75x vs TensorFlow Lite about 41x (about 1.8x).
hardware: 2018 Mac Mini, Intel Core i7-8700B @ 3.20 GHz
stars_or_usage: 848 stars; used in many audio plugins (BYOD, Chow Centaur, NeuralNote)
tradeoffs: Small fixed set of layer types (Dense, Conv1D/2D, GRU, LSTM, pooling, batch norm, common activations) and inference only; models are exported to JSON; header library with Eigen, xsimd or STL backends (Eigen best for larger networks, xsimd for small ones); designed for real-time audio, single-sample processing.
caveats: Numbers are only in plots, so every ratio is my approximation. The benchmark is by the RTNeural author, on one x86 Mac, with prebuilt ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite binaries and no stated compiler flags; layers are tiny, so per-call framework overhead dominates the baselines, and the advantage shrinks as layer size grows (STL backend falls to about the ONNX Runtime level at size 64 for GRU/LSTM). The reference paper (arXiv:2106.03037) was not opened.
found_via: WebSearch 'header-only C++ neural network inference library benchmark faster than TensorFlow Lite ONNX Runtime github README' (RTNeural-compare repo).

name: SageAttention
workload: Quantized (INT8, FP8, INT4) attention kernels for inference on Ampere, Ada, Hopper and RTX 50 GPUs, measured as attention TOPS and end-to-end model speed.
claimed_speedup: README news item: 'On RTX5090, SageAttention reaches 560T, 2.7x faster than FlashAttention2!'; on Hopper it matches the speed of FlashAttention3-FP8 with better accuracy. GitHub repository description: 'speedup of 2-5x compared to FlashAttention, without losing end-to-end metrics across language, image, and video models'. Detailed speed plots are images.
hardware: RTX 5090, RTX 4090, H100/H800/H20, A100, L20, L40, A6000, RTX 3090 (varies per plot)
tradeoffs: INT8/FP8 quantized attention: accuracy is preserved per the papers but is lossy; plug-and-play replacement for scaled-dot-product attention in PyTorch; GPU only, PyTorch 2.3+, CUDA 12+; v2 needs a source build.
caveats: Peer review is stated in the README (SageAttention ICLR 2025, SageAttention2 ICML 2025, SageAttention3 NeurIPS 2025 spotlight); the papers themselves could not be opened here. The code is mostly Python/Triton/CUDA with a PyTorch API, not a C++ library. The 2.7x figure is for one GPU and one baseline (FlashAttention2), and on Hopper it only matches FlashAttention3-FP8. The PyPI wheel carries a BSD-3-Clause license string while the repository LICENSE is Apache-2.0.
found_via: PyPI JSON page https://pypi.org/pypi/sageattention/json (attention kernels distributed through PyPI).

name: tiny-ml-runtime
workload: Single-sample inference of a 4-8-3 Iris MLP and a 784-128-10 MNIST MLP, pure C engine versus PyTorch called from a single-threaded Python loop.
claimed_speedup: Iris (4-8-3): pure C 2,732,240 predictions/s vs PyTorch 10,596 predictions/s (258x, as stated; 1M iterations 0.366 s vs 94.374 s). MNIST (784-128-10): pure C 4,244 vs PyTorch 22,502 predictions/s, i.e. PyTorch 5x faster.
tradeoffs: Naive C loops with no SIMD, tiling or threading; dense layers, ReLU and softmax only; weights exported from PyTorch to a binary file.
caveats: Educational project. The README itself says the 258x figure measures Python plus PyTorch dispatch overhead on a 4-feature input, not computational throughput, and that the gap disappears with batching, and on MNIST PyTorch wins by 5x. Included only because toy projects are in scope; likely a keep-with-shortcomings or reject for the verifier.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ library faster than XNNPACK OR oneDNN inference kernels benchmark GitHub' follow-up query for 'tiny-ml-runtime ... 258x faster than PyTorch'.

name: FlashInfer
baseline: FlashAttention-2/3, cuDNN, CUTLASS, TensorRT-LLM kernels (as selectable backends)
workload: LLM serving attention (paged/ragged KV cache, prefill, decode, MLA), GEMM, fused MoE, sampling and normalization kernels on Turing through Blackwell GPUs.
claimed_speedup: README states 'state-of-the-art performance' with optimized kernels for prefill, decode and mixed batching and automatic backend selection; no numbers in the README or in the benchmarks/README.md harness (flashinfer_benchmark.py compares fa2, fa3, cudnn, cutlass, trtllm backends and prints per-run timings only).
stars_or_usage: 6.5k stars; powers vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, TGI, MLC-LLM; PyPI flashinfer-python 0.7.0.post1 uploaded 2026-09-29
tradeoffs: Library plus kernel generator with JIT compilation; Python/PyTorch API with CUDA C++ kernels; FP8/FP4 low-precision support; NVIDIA GPUs only.
caveats: Tier D: no numbers on any page I could open. The MLSys 2025 paper (arXiv:2501.01005, cited in the README) and the flashinfer.ai blog posts were not reachable from this container, so a verifier should open them; the paper is expected to give measured speedups versus Triton/FlashAttention backends. last_commit not captured (commits page truncated); active status is inferred from the 2026-09-29 PyPI upload. Language split of the repo not confirmed.
found_via: PyPI JSON page https://pypi.org/pypi/flashinfer-python/json (kernel library distributed on PyPI).
